content: Countries with existing laboratory infrastructure capable of supporting routine pretreatment HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) testing often face challenges in procuring generic antiretroviral (ARV) drugs. This creates a significant cost differential between non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based and non-NNRTI-based regimens, which becomes a critical factor in HIV program planning. In such settings, implementing pretreatment HIVDR testing may be a more cost-effective option compared to introducing non-NNRTI-based regimens. The acceptability of HIVDR testing varies. Program managers and healthcare providers in middle-income countries generally find the intervention acceptable, whereas it is less so in low-income countries. Equity in access to non-NNRTI regimens is likely to improve outcomes for individuals at higher risk of NNRTI treatment failure due to pretreatment HIVDR. Establishing a new HIVDR genotype laboratory in lowand middle-income countries involves significant initial costs, estimated at approximately $600,000. This includes expenses for software, laboratory equipment, and an initial stock of reagents. Once operational, the cost per HIVDR test must be considered. A 2016 survey of 31 WHO-designated laboratories revealed that in-house assays were the most commonly used, with costs ranging from $40 to $317 per test. Laboratories using ViroSeq™ reported costs between $125 and $460 per test. These figures exclude labor, equipment maintenance, specimen transport, genotype interpretation, and result reporting costs. The cost of resistance testing kits has decreased in recent years, with some kits now available for as little as $50 per test in resource-limited settings. Future advancements in user-friendly, point-of-care HIVDR testing technologies may further reduce costs and expand accessibility. Cost-effectiveness analyses indicate that pretreatment HIVDR testing improves clinical outcomes in high-income countries when NNRTI-based regimens are used as first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART). Models from Brazil and Kenya suggest that HIVDR testing can enhance clinical outcomes and, in some cases, be cost-saving. For instance, the Brazilian model assumes that HIVDR testing at treatment initiation minimizes the use of more expensive regimens. However, this model does not account for costs related to specimen collection, transport, and personnel training. The Kenyan model estimates cost-effectiveness at $230 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY), assuming low-cost HIVDR testing is available. In sub-Saharan Africa, introducing pretreatment HIVDR testing (using dolutegravir [DTG] for individuals with NNRTI resistance) is predicted to yield better outcomes compared to continuing efavirenz (EFV)-based first-line ART. However, at the current projected cost of $44 per person per year for DTG, pretreatment HIVDR testing is not cost-effective compared to universal DTG-based regimens for all new ART initiators. If DTG costs exceed $100 per person per year, pretreatment HIVDR testing could become the more cost-effective option, depending on the prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR. The feasibility of pretreatment HIVDR testing is limited in lowand middle-income countries. A WHO-led survey in 2017 found that only 31% of program managers in ten such countries considered pretreatment HIVDR testing feasible. Key challenges include cost, result interpretation, delays in receiving results, and ensuring patient retention during the waiting period. Additionally, maintaining an adequate stock of alternative first-line ART regimens remains a concern. Countries with a pretreatment HIVDR prevalence of ≥10% among individuals initiating first-line ART should urgently consider alternative first-line regimens that do not include NNRTIs. If non-NNRTI regimens cannot be implemented at scale, pretreatment HIVDR testing can guide regimen selection. This threshold was established based on evidence of the negative treatment outcomes associated with pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs and the feasibility of measuring prevalence using available survey methods. The cost of conducting a national pretreatment HIVDR survey using WHO-standardized methods is approximately $240,000, assuming a sample size of 460 specimens from 20 ART sites and genotyping costs of $150 per specimen. Costs can be reduced if countries utilize WHO HIVResNet laboratories offering genotyping at no or reduced cost. Despite the investment, the benefits of such surveys, particularly in countries with large ART programs, justify the expense. In summary, the establishment of a 10% threshold for pretreatment HIVDR prevalence to NNRTIs signals the urgency of public health action. Countries with documented prevalence below this threshold should implement HIVDR prevention activities to minimize resistance.
